cards.text: Pull up a stool, friend. This psalm is for the choirmaster, and it comes from the sons of Korah, a family from the tribe of Levi (Numbers 16:1). The writer opens with a picture: a deer panting for streams of water, and that deer is THIRSTY.

cards.question: The psalm writer says his soul longs just like that thirsty deer. What is his soul longing for?

cards.text: And he's not thirsty for just anybody. His soul thirsts for the living God, and he asks, “When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?”

cards.question: The writer’s question shows he is already standing in God’s presence.

cards.text: Things are rough. His tears have been his food, day and night, and friend, I spent YEARS lying on old takeout menus in a junk drawer, and not ONE of them had that on it.

cards.question: While the writer cries day and night, what do people keep asking him all day long?

cards.text: As he pours out his soul, he remembers walking with the crowd to the house of God, and not in the back either. He was out front LEADING the procession!

cards.question: Back then, what was that walk to the house of God like?

answers.text: Full of shouts of joy and praise

cards.text: Then the writer turns and talks to his OWN soul: “Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me?” Back in my junk drawer days I never gave my soul a talking-to, friend. I just lay there and let the DUST win.

cards.question: The writer tells his downcast soul to put its ___ in God.
Even while his soul is downcast, the writer says he will praise God again.

cards.text: But one pep talk doesn't flip a switch. Right away he tells God, “my soul despairs within me.”

cards.question: With his soul in despair, the writer tells God that he ___ Him.

cards.text: He remembers God from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon, even from Mount Mizar. Then the picture turns to water: deep calls to deep, and breakers and waves roll right over him.

cards.question: The writer says the breakers and waves rolling over him are God’s own waves.
Earlier, tears were the writer’s food day and night. Now, even with the waves over him, what does he say comes by day and by night?

answers.text: The LORD’s love and His song

cards.text: Then he talks to God and calls Him “my Rock”, solid and steady. But the very next words out of his mouth are a hard question.

cards.question: The writer asks God, his Rock, why He has ___ him.

cards.text: He also asks why he must walk in sorrow because of the enemy’s oppression, and his enemies taunt him like the crushing of his bones. Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer feeling forgotten, so I get every word of this.
Then that line again: “Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me?” He tells his soul to put its hope in God, and this time he calls God “my Savior and my God.”
On to the next psalm. The writer asks God to vindicate him and plead his case against an ungodly nation.

cards.question: Who does the writer ask God to deliver him from?

cards.text: Then he tells God who He is to him, and right after that he asks, “Why have You rejected me?”

cards.question: Right before asking why God has rejected him, what does the writer call God?
The writer also asks the exact same question from the last psalm: “Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy’s oppression?”

cards.text: Then he asks God to send out His light and His truth. Take it from a stamper who spent years in a dark drawer, friend: LIGHT is exactly the right thing to ask for.

cards.question: The writer wants God’s light and truth to lead him to God’s holy ___.

cards.text: Once he gets there, he says he'll go to the altar of God. This man went from tears for FOOD to planning his route to the altar, and I am HERE for it!

cards.question: At the altar, the writer calls God his greatest ___.
The man who longed to appear in God’s presence now pictures himself praising God at His altar.

cards.text: And one last time, that line: “Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me?” That answer again, friend: hope in God, because he will yet praise Him, his Savior and his God.

findings.problem: The right answer 'God Himself' is the only Bible-sounding answer in a psalm. 'Peace and quiet' and 'A fresh start' sound like modern self-help, so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The core action of Psalm 42:3 is grief: crying day and night while people mock. The joke's comparison, takeout menus that don't list tears, only plays on the word 'food' and doesn't share that action. It also makes the psalmist's grief the punchline.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: In Psalm 42:10 the enemies repeat the taunt 'Where is your God?' from 42:3. No card tells this, so the baker misses that the mocking comes back.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The statement says the question is 'the exact same question from the last psalm.' The right answer (True) depends on both Psalm 42:9 and Psalm 43:2, but the card cites only Psalm 43:2.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower. A choice card cites only the verses of its right answer.

findings.problem: Psalm 43 has no heading of its own. Stop 2 treats its speaker as the same man as Psalm 42's. Card 10 says 'The man who longed to appear in God's presence' (Psalm 42:2), and cards 1 and 5 call him 'the writer' and point back to 'the last psalm.' The shared refrain suggests one speaker, but the text never says so.
findings.question: When Psalm 42 and 43 are taught as one passage, can Papa Dorin treat them as one speaker, as something the shared refrain clearly implies? Or must that connection be left open?

findings.problem: 4 of the 5 true-or-false cards are True (stop 1 cards 11 and 15, stop 2 cards 5 and 10). Only stop 1 card 4 is False. A baker could learn to pick True without reading.
findings.question: Should there be a rule about balancing True and False answers across a walkthrough?
